item.title: Tropical and maximum colorful matchings in vertex-colored graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.34107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A subgraph of a vertex-colored graph istropical if it contains every color. We study matchings by the number of colors they cover. A matching is maximum colorful if no matching covers more colors. When a tropical matching exists, the maximum colorful matchings are exactly the tropical matchings. We give polynomial-time algorithms for two problems: a maximum matching that covers the most colors, and a tropical matching with the fewest edges. Both algorithms rest on a counterpart of Berge's theorem: a matching is optimal if and only if it admits no tropical augmentation, or no tropical reduction. These are chains of alternating paths linked by relays, and each one is found by a single augmenting-path search in an auxiliary graph. The same tools give a maximum colorful matching with the fewest edges, and show that all maximum matchings that are maximum colorful are connected by flips. Finally, the sets of colors that a matching can cover form a matroid. The greedy algorithm then computes a matching of maximum color weight. This paper extends the conference version and the PhD thesis of one of the authors.
item.dc:creator: Johanne Cohen, Yannis Manoussakis, Hong Phong Pham, Zsolt Tuza

item.title: On the Hardness of Optimal CNOT Circuits
item.description: arXiv:2611.34138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note revisits the computational problem of optimal CNOT synthesis: given an invertible binary matrix $A\in \mathsf{GL}(d,2)$ over the field of two elements and a budget $K$, decide if $A$ can be implemented with $\leq K$ CNOT gates. The $\mathsf{NP}$-completeness of this problem was recently published independently by Acuaviva, Acuaviva, and Acuaviva (arXiv:2608.03825) and by Li and Guan (arXiv:2609.04160). This note gives a new proof, with three features. First, $\mathsf{NP}$-completeness holds even over linear oracles, i.e., matrices of the form $(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\mapsto(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}+F\mathbf{x})$, which are the standard reversible embedding of a linear function $F$. These are involutions, and seemingly simpler than the families of the two previous works, which both have order four. Second, hardness persists when SWAP gates are free and qubits may be permuted (and this holds under any connected topology). Third, the exposition is arguably simpler to follow. Along the way, it gives a proof of the XOR-circuit lower bound of Boyar, Matthews, and Peralta [J. Cryptology 26 (2013)] that is, perhaps, simpler than existing ones.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Pavlogiannis

item.title: New Insights into the Parameterized Complexity of Cutwidth
item.description: arXiv:2611.34501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Cutwidth problem asks for a linear ordering of the vertices that minimizes the maximum number of edges crossing between two consecutive positions. The problem is proven to be NP-hard by Gavril [CISS '77], which motivated research in parameterized complexity. A previously claimed FPT result for Cutwidth and Imbalance parameterized by twin cover by Gorzny and Buss [COCOON '19] was later invalidated. Misra and Mittal [Theor. Comput. Sci. '21] clarified this issue, proved that Imbalance is in XP parameterized by twin cover and in FPT parameterized by $\omega$-bounded twin cover, i.e., where the size of the cliques outside the twin cover are bounded by $\omega$. The analogous questions remained open for cutwidth. In this work, we answer one of them by showing that Cutwidth is FPT parameterized by $\omega$-bounded twin cover. Additionally, we present an XP algorithm for Cutwidth parameterized by vertex integrity and prove W[1]-hardness for the parameter treedepth.
item.dc:creator: Klara Jacobsen, Klaus Jansen, Lis Pirotton, Bj\"orn Schumacher

item.title: The asymptotic spectrum of tensors is connected
item.description: arXiv:2611.34664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove path-connectedness of the asymptotic spectrum of complex tensors of every fixed order $k \geq 3$: every spectral point is connected by a path to every "one leg versus the rest" flattening rank. In particular, the asymptotic spectrum evaluated at any fixed tensor is a closed interval, answering a question of Strassen. This was previously known only on specific families of tensors (Strassen, FOCS 1986, Crelle 1987-1991; Wigderson and Zuiddam, Bull. AMS 2026) or for specific families of spectral points (Christandl, Vrana and Zuiddam, STOC 2018; Sakabe, Do\u{g}an and Walter, FOCS 2026; Alman, Li and Pratt, FOCS 2026). To obtain our path-connectedness theorem we develop a general method for "interpolating" between spectral points, which applies to Strassen semirings that are appropriately decomposable (in the sense of an information-theoretic "method of types" on the semiring) and whose spectral points satisfy a cover property (inspired by slice rank). This covers tensors and asymptotic rank (with "types" given by decomposition into symmetric group irreps), as well as other objects and asymptotic problems, like graphs and Shannon capacity, where it matches the interpolation of Vrana (2019). Using our interpolation methods we furthermore obtain new results and simpler proofs of previous results regarding the asymptotic spectrum of rectangular matrix multiplication, polynomial multiplication and non-crossing (laminar) quantum functionals.
item.dc:creator: P\'eter Vrana, Jeroen Zuiddam

item.title: Low-degree hardness rules out eigenvalue tests but not eigenvector tests
item.description: arXiv:2611.34728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study what low-degree hardness implies for spectral tests, with the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE) as the null distribution. We show that, once a fixed amount of Gaussian noise is added, it rules out every test based on eigenvalues, but not tests based on eigenvectors. For eigenvalues, if the low-degree advantage vanishes at logarithmic degree, then the joint law of the noisy eigenvalues converges to that of the GOE in total variation. For eigenvectors, we construct planted distributions with vanishing low-degree advantage whose eigenvalues follow the GOE law exactly at every noise level, yet whose noisy eigenvectors still distinguish them from the GOE. A single eigenvector can suffice. After a small amount of noise, a polynomial-time test that uses only the span of a fixed fraction of the top eigenvectors also succeeds, even when the low-degree advantage vanishes at a prescribed polylogarithmic degree. To prove the eigenvalue result, we split the noise into three increments. The first uses the low-degree assumption to establish eigenvalue rigidity. The second couples the two spectra through Dyson Brownian motion and applies homogenization to obtain a transport estimate. The third uses Gaussian smoothing to convert this estimate into closeness in total variation.
item.dc:creator: Xuan Chen, Shuangping Li

item.title: $\mathsf{AC}^0 \not\subseteq \mathsf{BQAC}^0/\mathsf{qpoly}$ via Sublinear-Degree Pauli Approximation
item.description: arXiv:2611.34803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove $\mathsf{AC}^0 \not\subseteq \mathsf{BQAC}^0/\mathsf{qpoly}$ in the single-copy, single-output model via an explicit $\mathsf{P}$-uniform family of linear-size monotone depth-2 CNFs. Every $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuit with arbitrary quantum advice achieves only an inverse-polynomial worst-case advantage over random guessing on this family. To prove this, we approximate the acceptance operator of any such circuit in operator norm by an advice-independent Hermitian operator of sublinear Pauli degree on a designated register alone, with degree exponent independent of width. Product-projection localization and Pauli twirling produce an auxiliary-register spectral cutoff that folds into contractions during backward peeling. The same approximation yields two stretched-exponential bounds against $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits on $m$-qubit states. First, given polynomially many copies and input-independent quantum advice, single-output circuits distinguish exact or exponentially approximate state $2$-designs from Haar-random states with advantage at most $e^{-m^\alpha}$. Second, any state prepared from fewer than $k$ arbitrary input qubits and remaining $|0\rangle$ inputs has spectral weight at most $2e^{-m^\alpha}$ in a constant-energy-density band of an Anshu--Breuckmann--Nirkhe NLTS Hamiltonian encoding $k$ logical qubits. Both bounds hold for every fixed $\alpha\in(0,1)$.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoming Sun, Jingheng Wang

item.title: Deterministic Verification and Computation of Real Matrix Products Have the Same Arithmetic Exponent
item.description: arXiv:2611.34814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given three $n\times n$ real matrices $A,B,C$, we ask whether $AB=C$. In an exact real arithmetic model that charges one step for each addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, comparison, or sign test, we prove that deterministic exact verification requires $\Omega(n^{\omega_{\mathbb{C}}})$ steps and has the same optimal arithmetic exponent $\omega_{\mathbb{C}}$ as matrix multiplication. Assuming the value $\omega_{\mathbb{C}}=9/4$ and the fixed-size border-rank lower bound stated in the OpenAI preprint of November 24, 2026, deterministic verification requires $\Omega(n^{9/4})$ steps, whereas Freivalds' randomized test uses $O(n^2)$ steps with one-sided error. More generally, if a tree of cost $s$ correctly decides $y=T(u,v)$ on all real inputs, the bilinear map $T$ is a coefficientwise limit of tensors of real rank $O(s)$.
item.dc:creator: Xiangle Chen

item.title: Winning and losing NoGo is PSPACE-complete
item.description: arXiv:2611.33127v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We resolve an open problem of Burke and Hearn and show that the combinatorial game NoGo is PSPACE-complete on grids. This is the usual geometry the game is played on, including at the tournament at a 2011 Banff workshop. In addition to this result, we show that it is also PSPACE-complete under mis\`ere play on grids. We prove both of these results using reductions from Bounded Two-Player Constraint Logic. Finally, we show that it is PSPACE-complete under normal play on connected bipartite subcubic graphs.
item.dc:creator: Kyle Burke, Alfie Davies, Craig Tennenhouse

item.title: Approximate Counting and the Provability of Combinatorial Principles
item.description: arXiv:2611.33356v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding which axioms suffice for the provability of known results in algorithms and complexity and whether they can settle longstanding conjectures in these areas is a fundamental direction at the intersection of logic and computer science. Motivated by this research program and its applications, we investigate bounded arithmetic theories designed to serve as a logical foundation for *probabilistic reasoning*, the relation between these theories, and whether they can prove more theorems than their underlying base theory for *deterministic reasoning*. In more detail, for nearly twenty years, Je\v{r}\'abek's theory $\mathsf{APC}_1$ [Je\v{r}07a] has provided a standard framework for the formalization of results from theoretical computer science relying on probabilistic techniques. In a recent work, [CLOW26] introduced a (possibly weaker) theory called $\mathsf{APX}_1$. This theory is able to capture a large set of probabilistic arguments using four simple axioms for *approximate counting*. Both theories extend Cook's theory $\mathsf{PV}_1$ [Coo75] for deterministic polynomial-time reasoning. Our main result establishes that, in the relativized setting, $\mathsf{APX}_1$ does not prove the retraction weak pigeonhole principle ($\mathsf{rwPHP}$). Consequently, $\mathsf{APC}_1$ is not conservative over $\mathsf{APX}_1$ with respect to relativized $\forall\Sigma^b_1$ sentences. Moreover, we establish that the unprovability of $\mathsf{rwPHP}$ is part of a more general phenomenon: for a large class of finite combinatorial principles, the existence of an *infinite model* of the negation of the principle *characterizes* its unprovability in $\mathsf{APX}_1$. This result, which is analogous to a theorem of Riis [Rii94], implies that $\mathsf{PV}_1$ and $\mathsf{APX}_1$ prove exactly the same finite combinatorial principles of this form.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Korten, Jiatu Li, Igor C. Oliveira, Hanlin Ren

item.title: Fast Algorithms for Permanents of Permutationally-Dominant Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2611.33485v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We establish a fast algorithm for approximating the permanent of permutationally-dominant matrices. In particular, we obtain a fully polynomial randomised approximation scheme whose runtime is quadratic in both the dimension of the matrix and the inverse of the approximation error. Our approach is based on a polymer model representation of the permanent and importance sampling of the logarithm of its partition function via the theory of heaps of pieces of Viennot.
item.dc:creator: Ryan L. Mann

item.title: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the ROM
item.description: arXiv:2611.33508v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Nearly five decades after their introduction, Merkle trees remain the most efficient hash-based vector commitments. They compress a vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ into a commitment whose size is independent of $n$, such that a verifier can open any bit $x_i$ using $\log n$ hash evaluations. The security of the scheme (intractability of finding two distinct openings for a given bit using the same commitment) follows from the collision resistance of the hash function. The verifier's runtime complexity is a bottleneck in many key applications of vector commitments, including SNARKs, credentials, and authenticated dictionaries. As such, a longstanding open question has been whether it is possible to construct hash-based vector commitments where the verifier makes a sublogarithmic number of hash evaluations. We prove that sublogarithmic verifier complexity is impossible to achieve through black-box use of a hash function; we not only rule out constructions from collision resistant hash functions, but in fact show that commitment schemes with sublogarithmic verifier complexity are unachievable in the random oracle model. In particular, any vector commitment with deterministic verifiers has verifier query complexity $\Omega_{\theta}(\log n)$, where $\theta$ is the input length of the random oracle. This bound is matched up to constant factors by high-arity Merkle trees. The key technical lemma in our proof is a disjoint product lemma, which can be viewed as a computational analog of the van den Berg-Kesten-Reimer (BKR) inequality. We believe this lemma is of independent interest, and in particular may be useful for showing other lower bounds and separations in the random oracle model.
item.dc:creator: Miranda Christ, Oliver Korten, Tal Malkin, Noam Mazor, Shyamal Patel

item.title: Almost Tight Hardness of Approximation for $0$-Extension
item.description: arXiv:2611.33928v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the $0$-Extension problem, we are given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with non-negative edge weights $w: E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, a collection $T \subseteq V$ of $k$ terminals, and a metric $D$ over terminals $T$. The goal is to find a retraction $f:V\rightarrow T$ that maps every terminal to itself, while minimizing the sum over all edges of the product of the edge's weight and the distance in $D$ between the terminals to which its endpoints are assigned, i.e., \[ \sum_{\{u,v\}\in E} w_{\{u,v\}} \cdot D(f(u), f(v)). \] Fakcharoenphol, Harrelson, Rao, and Talwar achieve the best known approximation ratio of $O(\log k / \log \log k)$, while the known approximation hardness is $\Omega(\sqrt{\log k})$ assuming the unique games conjecture. In this work, we establish an $\Omega(\log^{1-\varepsilon}k)$ hardness of approximation for every constant $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$ and arbitrarily large fixed $k$, almost matching the upper bound in the exponent of $\log k$. The main technical contribution is an $\Omega(\log^{1-\varepsilon}k)$ integrality gap for the earthmover relaxation. Our construction is inspired by randomized extensions of expanders introduced by Schwartz and Tur for the metric relaxation. The result then follows from an existing theorem by Manokaran, Naor, Raghavendra, and Schwartz that translates the integrality gap for the earthmover relaxation to the approximation hardness for every fixed $k$.
item.dc:creator: Qingyun Chen, Weihao Zhu

item.title: Deterministic integer factorization from abundance decisions
item.description: arXiv:2611.34242v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove that deciding whether a positive integer is abundant is equivalent to complete integer factorization under deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. In particular, abundance can be decided in deterministic polynomial time if and only if integers can be factored in deterministic polynomial time. Our reduction uses carefully chosen coprime multipliers to recover exact divisor sums from abundance queries, and then extracts the complete prime factorization of an integer $n$ deterministically from the divisor sums of $O(\log n)$ consecutive powers of $n$. Altogether, factoring $n$ requires $O((\log n)^4)$ adaptive abundance queries, each at an integer of $O((\log n)^6)$ binary digits.
item.dc:creator: Joseph M. Shunia

item.title: From NP-Hardness to Exact Tractability Through Sample Abundance
item.description: arXiv:2611.34734v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Additional observations can make exact optimization tractable without changing the objective or feasible set. We establish this phenomenon for noisy parity fitting, a worst-case NP-hard problem, with uniformly sampled rank-one sign tensor entries, independent fair factor signs and independent errors. For fixed interaction order $k\ge3$, $n$ signs per block, logarithmic mean degree and known channel biases, $O(n/(\log n)^{1/(k-2)})$ further readings of the same source suffice with high probability for exact optimization in $O(n\log^2 n)$ worst-case work. The leading coefficient is sharp for weak recovery by depth-$O(\log\log n)$ local estimators with independent reading marks. A common signed-field law determines the gain over the generating source, the number of tied optima and the dimension needed for later reweightings. The geometry of the remaining coordinates determines the sharp radius of local verification for high-scoring assignments with high probability.
item.dc:creator: Mojtaba Soltanalian

item.title: Unitary Synthesis with a Unary Tracker
item.description: arXiv:2611.34740v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This manuscript studies general unitary synthesis using unary-encoded ancillary register. Our first construction focuses on the $T$-cost of unitary synthesis. We maintain a unary register that coherently tracks the computational-basis label of the data. This allows Boolean lookups to use only CNOTs and shares the precision-dependent synthesis cost across the branches of each cosine-sine decomposition (CSD) factor. For a classically specified $n$-qubit unitary with $K$ mixing branches in its CSD, we obtain $T$-count $O(K+NL)$ using $N+O(L)$ clean ancillas, where $N=2^n$ and $L=n+\log(1/\epsilon)$. We also give a related construction that directly applies the unitary onto a unary register to implement disjoint branches in parallel. Combining this with the quantum Shannon decomposition gives space-depth volume $O(N^2)$ using arbitrary single-qubit gates and CNOTs, which matches the asymptotically optimal bound.
item.dc:creator: Fred Sun

item.title: Computing Normal-Form Correlated Equilibria in Extensive-Form Games is in PPAD
item.description: arXiv:2611.34897v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the computational complexity of finding any normal-form correlated equilibria (NFCE for short) in the succinct games of extensive-form with perfect recall, which is considered as a major open problem in algorithmic game theory. Our main results place this problem in PPAD for an arbitrary numbers of players. Our second result establishes PPAD-hardness of computing such an NFCE with support size of at most quadratic in the size of the game, even for two-player games. The posed restriction on the support size in PPAD-hardness construction is motivated by our PPAD algorithm, which constructs an NFCE with support size quadratic in the size of the input extensive-form game.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Cheval, Florian Horn, Soumyajit Paul, Mahsa Shirmohammadi

item.title: Bound Entanglement with Negative Partial Transpose Exists
item.description: arXiv:2611.34921v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that the Werner state $\rho = (23 I - 3\,\mathrm{SWAP})/1448$ on $\mathbb{C}^8 \otimes \mathbb{C}^8$ has a negative partial transpose and is bound entangled: no LOCC protocol can distill entanglement from any number of copies of $\rho$, and even with separable operations the fidelity of a two-qubit output with a Bell state never exceeds $(1+\sqrt{2})/4 \approx 0.604$. It follows that distillable entanglement is neither additive nor convex.
item.dc:creator: Islam Faisal

item.title: An elementary proof that linking problems are hard
item.description: arXiv:2509.13120v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a new, elementary proof of what we believe is the simplest known example of a "natural" problem in computational 3-dimensional topology that is NP-hard---namely, the Trivial Sublink Problem: given a diagram $L$ of a link in $S^3$ and a positive integer $k$, decide if $L$ contains a $k$ component sublink that is trivial. This problem was previously shown to be NP-hard in independent works of Koenig-Tsvietkova and de Mesmay-Rieck-Sedgwick-Tancer, both of which used reductions from 3SAT. The reduction we describe instead starts with the Independent Set Problem, and allows us to avoid the use of Brunnian links such as the Borromean rings. On the technical level, this entails a new conceptual insight: the Trivial Sublink Problem is hard entirely due to mod 2 pairwise linking, with no need for integral or higher order linking. On the pedagogical level, the reduction we describe is entirely elementary, and thus suitable for introducing undergraduates and non-experts to complexity-theoretic low-dimensional topology. To drive this point home, in this work we assume no familiarity with low-dimensional topology, and---other than Reidemeister's Theorem and Karp's result that the Clique Problem is NP-hard---we provide more-or-less complete definitions and proofs. We have also constructed a web app that accompanies this work and allows a user to visualize the new reduction interactively.
item.dc:creator: Shannon Cheng, Anna Chlopecki, Saarah Nazar, Eric Samperton

item.title: Parameterized Complexity of Finding a Maximum Common Vertex Subgraph Without Isolated Vertices
item.description: arXiv:2602.10948v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we study the Maximum Common Vertex Subgraph problem: Given two input graphs $G_1,G_2$ and a non-negative integer $h$, is there a common subgraph $H$ on at least $h$ vertices such that there is no isolated vertex in $H$. In other words, each connected component of $H$ has at least $2$ vertices. This problem naturally arises in graph theory along with other variants of the well-studied Maximum Common Subgraph problem and also has applications in computational social choice. We show that this problem is NP-hard and provide an FPT algorithm when parameterized by $h$. Next, we conduct a study of the problem on common structural parameters like vertex cover number, maximum degree, treedepth, pathwidth and treewidth of one or both input graphs. We derive a complete dichotomy of parameterized results for our problem with respect to individual parameterizations as well as combinations of parameterizations from the above structural parameters. This provides us with a deep insight into the complexity theoretic and parameterized landscape of this problem.
item.dc:creator: Palash Dey, Anubhav Dhar, Ashlesha Hota, Sudeshna Kolay, Aritra Mitra

item.title: Fine-Grained AC$^0$ Lower Bounds for $k$-OV, $k$-XOR, and $k$-SUM via Colored Subgraph Isomorphism
item.description: arXiv:2608.08578v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the circuit cost of selecting $k$ objects satisfying orthogonality, zero XOR, or modular zero SUM. Our main lower bounds in nonuniform AC$^0$ use a common framework of depth-zero projections from colored subgraph isomorphism. The projections use dimension, row count, or bit width $O(k\log n)$ and preserve circuit size, depth, and gate orientation. Stronger lower bounds for suitable source patterns transfer through the same framework to all three targets. Our XOR lower bounds require odd $k$. For every fixed depth $d$ and sufficiently large fixed $k$, we prove unconditional lower bounds $n^{\Omega(k)}$ for OV and $(n/k)^{\Omega(k)}$ for XOR and SUM, with an absolute constant in the exponent independent of $d$ and $k$; only the threshold on $n$ may depend on $(d,k)$. For $k\to\infty$ with $k=n^{o(1)}$, combining our projections with Beame's small-clique lower bound yields $n^{\Omega_d(\min\{\sqrt{k},\log n\})}$ at every fixed depth $d$. For circuits of depth at most three with either type of output gate, we strengthen the exponent to $\Omega(k)$. At dimension, row count, or bit width $\Theta(k\log n)$ with sufficiently large constant factors, all three problems admit depth-three circuits with a top OR gate. Their sizes match our lower bounds for unrestricted depth three up to constants in the exponent for sufficiently large $k$ and $n\ge k^C$ with a suitable constant $C>1$.
item.dc:creator: Haoxing Lin

item.title: On the Parameterized Complexity of Coloring Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2609.09837v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coloring Discovery asks whether a possibly improper initial coloring can be made proper within a prescribed number of allowed changes. We study the parameterized complexity of three modification step models that were studied previously in the literature: recoloring one vertex (color flipping), swapping the colors of arbitrary vertices (color swapping), and swapping colors only across an edge (color sliding). For color flipping, we give exact fixed-parameter algorithms for the parameters vertex cover and distance to complete. For color swapping, we obtain fixed-parameter tractability for the parameter vertex cover plus the number of colors. Our lower bounds show W[1]-hardness for treedepth plus feedback vertex set in the color flipping model and for the number of colors plus bandwidth or distance to disjoint paths in the swapping and sliding models. All three variants remain NP-complete with four colors on graphs of diameter two.
item.dc:creator: Eric Decker, Sebastian Siebertz

item.title: Degree-bounded Satisfiability of Local MPNNs with Sum Aggregation is NEXPTIME-hard
item.description: arXiv:2611.32595v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove that the following problem is NEXPTIME-hard: given a message passing neural network (MPNN) $M$ with local sum aggregation and truncated ReLU activations, and a degree bound $d$ encoded in unary, decide whether there is a pointed graph $(G,v)$ with rational node labels and degree at most $d$ that is accepted by $M$. Hardness already holds for the fixed degree bound $d=3$.
item.dc:creator: Marco S\"alzer

item.title: Space Complexity Dichotomies for Subgraph Finding Problems in the Streaming Model
item.description: arXiv:2602.08002v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the space complexity of four variants of the standard subgraph finding problem in the streaming model. Specifically, given an $n$-vertex input graph and a fixed pattern graph on at least three vertices, we consider two settings: undirected simple graphs, denoted by $G$ and $H$, and oriented graphs, denoted by $\vec{G}$ and $\vec{H}$. Depending on the setting, the task is to decide whether $G$ contains $H$ as a subgraph or as an induced subgraph, or whether $\vec{G}$ contains $\vec{H}$ as a subgraph or as an induced subgraph. Let $\textsc{Sub}(H)$, $\textsc{IndSub}(H)$, $\textsc{Sub}(\vec{H})$, and $\textsc{IndSub}(\vec{H})$ denote these four variants, respectively. An oriented graph is well-oriented if it admits a bipartition in which every arc is oriented from the same part to the other, and a vertex is internal if both its in-degree and out-degree are non-zero. For each variant, we obtain a complete dichotomy theorem, briefly summarized as follows. \begin{itemize} \item $\textsc{Sub}(H)$ can be solved by an $\tilde{O}(1)$-pass $n^{2-\Omega(1)}$-space algorithm if and only if $H$ is bipartite. \item $\textsc{IndSub}(H)$ can be solved by an $\tilde{O}(1)$-pass $n^{2-\Omega(1)}$-space algorithm if and only if $H$ is $P_3$, $P_4$, or $\mbox{co-}P_3$. \item $\textsc{Sub}(\vec{H})$ can be solved by a deterministic single-pass $n^{2-\Omega(1)}$-space algorithm if and only if every connected component of $\vec H$ is either a well-oriented bipartite graph or a tree containing at most one internal vertex. \item $\textsc{IndSub}(\vec{H})$ can be solved by an $\tilde{O}(1)$-pass $n^{2-\Omega(1)}$-space algorithm if and only if the underlying undirected simple graph $H$ is a $\mbox{co-}P_3$. \end{itemize} All our upper bounds are attained by deterministic algorithms that find a copy, whereas all our lower bounds hold even for randomized algorithms that only detect one.S
item.dc:creator: Yu-Sheng Shih, Meng-Tsung Tsai, Yen-Chu Tsai, Ying-Sian Wu

item.title: Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization Beyond $1/e$ with Feasible Gradient Queries
item.description: arXiv:2609.02145v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets $K\subseteq[0,1]^d$ when gradients may be queried only at feasible points. The online approximation coefficients $4/9$ (Aggarwal and Lu) and $2\sqrt{3}-3\approx 0.4641$ (Aggarwal and Du) rely on queries along chains that start from the all-ones vector and leave $K$. With every query in $K$, the best known coefficient was $1/e$. We give an online algorithm with coefficient $0.4013$ that, in each round, plays a random action, queries one gradient at a point of $K$, and makes one projection. Its expected approximate regret is $O(RB(1+R)\sqrt{T})$, where $R\le\sqrt{d}$ bounds the norm of points of $K$ and $B$ bounds the gradient norm on $K$. For a budget $\sum_i x_i\le k$, the bound is $O(kB\sqrt{T})$. The algorithm keeps a state $x\in K$, and the analysis applies the coordinate-chain comparison of Aggarwal and Lu inside the box $[0,x]$, which keeps every query feasible. A second comparison, along a path from $0$ in the direction $x$, cancels the extra terms that the box creates. Because the queries are feasible, they can be played, which gives regret $O(T^{2/3})$ under semi-bandit feedback and $O(T^{4/5})$ under bandit feedback with bounded values. Unbiased stochastic gradients with bounded second moment keep the $\sqrt{T}$ rate, and on a fixed function the algorithm attains $0.4013\,\mathrm{OPT}-\varepsilon$ in expectation with $O(1+R^2(1+R)^2B^2/\varepsilon^2)$ feasible gradient queries.
item.dc:creator: Vaneet Aggarwal, Yiyang Lu

item.title: A Note on Binary Quadratic Systems and their relation to complexity theory
item.description: arXiv:2609.07769v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deciding whether a system of multivariate quadratic equations over $\mathbb F_2$ has a solution is a classical NP-complete problem, and remains so for square systems, with as many equations as variables. The hardness of this problem is one of the cornerstones of nowadays post-quantum cryptography. Let $\mathrm{MQ}_0(n)$ and $\mathrm{MQ}_1(n)$ denote the sets of square quadratic systems in $n$ variables having respectively no solutions and exactly one solution. $\cup_{n\geq 2} \mathrm{MQ}_0(n)$ is a coNP-complete language, while $\cup_{n\geq 2} \mathrm{MQ}_1(n)$ lies in DP. It is known that $\lim_{n\to \infty} |\mathrm{MQ}_1(n)|/|\mathrm{MQ}_0(n)|=1$. Here we prove the explicit finite-$n$ bounds \[ |\mathrm{MQ}_0(n)|<|\mathrm{MQ}_1(n)| \le \left(1+\frac{1}{2^n-1}\right)|\mathrm{MQ}_0(n)|, \] More generally, let $Q_d$ be the space of polynomial functions $(\mathbb{F}_2)^n\to\mathbb F_2$ of degree at most $d$, and let $\alpha_k$ count square systems in $(Q_d)^n$ having exactly $k$ solutions. Then \[ \alpha_0<\alpha_1 \le \left(1+\frac{1}{2^n-1}\right)\alpha_0\,, \qquad 2\le d\le n \,. \] The proof combines matroid and coding-theoretic methods. We interpret $(\mathbb{F}_2)^n$ as the ground set of the evaluation matroid of $Q_d$, express $\alpha_0$ and $\alpha_1$ through characteristic polynomials, and use a Whitney-type sign-reversing involution to show that the only terms that can push $\alpha_1-\alpha_0$ below $\alpha_1/2^n$ come from the elements of a matroid port. These are identified with minimal-support words of the Reed--Muller code $\mathrm{RM}(n-d-1,n)=\mathrm{RM}(d,n)^\perp$; the required estimate then follows from the MacWilliams identity, the minimum-distance bound $2^{d+1}$, and the even-weight structure of the code.
item.dc:creator: Gabriele Radici, Massimiliano Sala

item.title: Complexity of Autobidding Equilibria in GSP Sponsored Shopping
item.description: arXiv:2610.13716v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We revisit autobidding equilibria in GSP sponsored shopping auctions, recently proposed and studied in D\"utting et al. We establish computational upper bounds for both budget constraints (ABE-B) and return-on-investment constraints (ABE-R): computing an exact equilibrium is in FIXP, while computing a $\gamma$-approximate equilibrium is in PPAD even for inverse-exponentially small $\gamma$. At the same time, we establish tight inapproximability for both models: for every fixed $0\leq\gamma<1$, computing a $\gamma$-approximate equilibrium is PPAD-hard, even when all items are displayed and all click-through rates are equal. A key ingredient in our hardness reductions is a new variant of PureCircuit with bounded forward span, which we prove remains PPAD-hard. This structural restriction makes our reduction parameters independent of circuit size, enabling hardness for every fixed $\gamma<1$. More broadly, our approach suggests a strategy for strengthening PPAD-hardness results in other settings, by developing structural insights into the target problem and new hardness-preserving restrictions on PureCircuit in tandem, with each informing the other and the design of the reduction.
item.dc:creator: Kristoffer Arnsfelt Hansen, Yuhao Li, Xinhao Nie

item.title: Undirected Multiple-Unicast Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
item.description: arXiv:2610.20079v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In undirected multiple-unicast networks, where independent messages are sent between specified source-destination pairs, network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas fractional routing splits and forwards individual messages along paths without mixing them. Proposed in 2004 by Li and Li and independently by Harvey, Kleinberg, and Lehman, the multiple-unicast conjecture---long a central open problem in network coding with deep connections to computational complexity---asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same achievable rate region. We construct a counterexample refuting this conjecture and use it to reduce block transfers in external-memory data rearrangement, thereby accelerating external-memory integer sorting and answering in the affirmative the longstanding question of Aggarwal and Vitter (1988) on whether integer operations can beat the comparison-sorting input/output (I/O) bound. Specifically, we give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $\Theta(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $$O\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right),$$ where $\varepsilon=1.5\times10^{-5}$ is an absolute constant. This bound asymptotically improves on the classical $\Theta\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log(N/M)}{\log(M/B)}\right]\right)$ comparison-sorting bound in certain parameter regimes. Under the external-memory model specified in this paper, we have formally verified the algorithm's correctness and I/O complexity bound in Lean 4. Our reduction is independent of the address-field interchange construction. Using the one from recent work on multitape integer multiplication gives the bound for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, with an $\varepsilon$-dependent constant.
item.dc:creator: Baochun Li, Zongpeng Li, Sirui Liu
